item.title: The first touchscreen Mac, one day later: touch can be switched off, and macOS is only starting to adapt
item.description:
A day after Apple unveiled its first touchscreen Mac, the details that matter most to skeptics are emerging — and they are reassuring. The new PROLED MacBook Pro includes an accessibility setting to turn touch input off entirely, plus an option for pinch-to-zoom across the interface, so nobody is forced into the new interaction model. When touch is on, macOS reshapes itself: menu bar items expand under a fingertip, window controls grow, and the Dynamic Island pulls down into a floating widget.

Apple says this is just the start of making macOS touch-friendly, and hardware chief John Ternus frames touch as an addition that must not make the Mac lesser in any way. The lineup now spans $1,999 to a fully loaded $14,549 (thanks to a new 16TB SSD option), and TrendForce expects up to 1.5 million OLED touchscreen MacBook Pros to ship in 2027. The message: touch is here, but the traditional Mac is not going anywhere.

item.title: New iPad mini: OLED without ProMotion, and Apple explains why
item.description:
The new iPad mini's OLED display is its headline upgrade, but one omission drew questions: no ProMotion, so refresh rate stays at 60Hz instead of up to 120Hz. In interviews, Apple's VP of hardware design David Pakula defended the choice, saying the OLED panel itself delivers the meaningful upgrade and that ProMotion remains exclusive to the iPad Pro among iPads for now. He also discussed the mini's thinner, lighter design and its Acoustic Display.

Separately, Xcode 27.2 quietly confirmed specs Apple never lists: the new iPad mini (A20 Pro) has 12GB of RAM, the same as the iPhone Duo, while the new Apple TV 4K (A19) has 8GB. With a memory-chip shortage pushing RAM prices up industry-wide, those figures are worth knowing — and they suggest Apple is not skimping on memory in its smallest devices.

item.title: Apple cuts App Store commission to 26% in Taiwan after regulator talks
item.description:
Apple will lower its standard App Store commission in Taiwan from 30% to 26% for in-app purchases and paid apps on iOS and iPadOS, effective October 31. The change follows discussions with the Taiwan Fair Trade Commission, and Apple framed it as reflecting its ongoing commitment to developers.

The cut is small — four percentage points — but it continues a pattern: regulators in individual markets are steadily chipping away at the 30% standard, with Japan having secured a similar outcome. For developers selling in Taiwan, it is a modest but real revenue improvement; for Apple, it is another sign that the global App Store fee structure is being renegotiated market by market rather than all at once.

item.title: Abandoned Popcorn Time updater left up to 350,000 Macs open to takeover
item.description:
If you installed Popcorn Time on a Mac years ago, part of it may still be running — and it could have handed attackers full control. Security researchers at Eye Research detailed how Time4Popcorn, an unofficial fork of the old torrent-streaming app, left behind a small updater that checked for updates on every boot, even for people who had not opened the app in years. The updater trusted whatever it downloaded and ran it with full system privileges.

Worse, the project was long abandoned, so its update infrastructure was effectively unguarded. Up to 350,000 Macs are estimated to have been exposed. The broader lesson: forgotten software with persistent background components is a real attack surface, and it is worth auditing old installs — especially anything that phones home at startup.

item.title: Russia orders Apple to hand over users' messages on demand
item.description:
Apple and Microsoft have been added to a Russian state surveillance registry that requires them to hand over users' text, video, and audio messages on request, without a legal process. WhatsApp and Telegram are already on the same list; it is unclear why Apple was only added now.

The move follows Russia's blocking of FaceTime in 2025 and continues the country's tightening control over private communications. Apple has not publicly commented on how it will respond, but the registry obligation sits in direct tension with the end-to-end encryption Apple markets for iMessage and FaceTime. For users in Russia, the practical question is what data Apple actually holds and can produce — and whether services get further restricted if Apple resists.

Sources

  • AppleInsider News: Russia orders Apple to surrender users' messages on demand

item.title: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17 billion
item.description:
DoorDash announced a deal to buy grocery-delivery rival Instacart for $17 billion, at $65 a share — a 26% premium over Instacart's October 22 closing price. The consideration will be at least 75% cash, with shareholders able to choose cash or DoorDash stock. The deal has not yet closed and will face regulatory review.

For users, the immediate effect is one fewer independent delivery option on the iPhone: two of the biggest app-based delivery platforms would become one company. Consolidation in delivery has historically meant fewer promotions and less competitive pressure on fees, though DoorDash will argue the combination lets it compete more effectively against larger rivals. Expect scrutiny from regulators given how much of the US delivery market the merged company would control.

Sources

  • AppleInsider News: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17 billion, slashing user options

item.title: iOS 27.2 brings Shortcuts upgrades and Multiview for iPhone Duo
item.description:
iOS 27.2, released this week, is more than a maintenance update. The Shortcuts app gets a batch of new and improved features alongside the Siri AI, FaceTime, and Messages upgrades, and the Apple TV app gains Multiview — a feature tailor-made for the iPhone Duo's foldable display, letting viewers watch multiple streams at once on the big inner screen.

Work on iOS 27.3 is already underway, with the next major iPhone update expected on Apple's usual cadence. For Duo owners still learning their device, Multiview is one of the first features that genuinely justifies the foldable form factor rather than merely adapting to it.

item.title: HomePod mini 2 arrives Friday, but its Siri AI upgrade will come later
item.description:
After more than two weeks of pre-orders, the HomePod mini 2 begins arriving to customers and hits stores Friday, October 30. The new model runs on the Apple Watch Series 10's S-series chip and adds two-tone color options — for pink, blue, and green models, the outer and inner acoustic fabrics are different colors (blue outside with green underneath, and vice versa for green).

One thing buyers will not get on day one: Siri AI. The more intelligent, personalized Siri powered by Apple Intelligence is promised for a future software update, with no date given. If you are buying the mini 2 primarily for the smarter assistant, expect to wait — the hardware is here, but the headline software feature is not yet.

item.title: Apple unveils its first touchscreen Mac: the OLED MacBook Pro
item.description:
Apple broke one of its longest-standing taboos, announcing 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pros with a touch-enabled PROLED XDR display — tandem OLED technology Apple calls the best display ever in a pro laptop, with up to 1,600 nits-class brightness, striking contrast, and vivid color. The machines run M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, are slightly thinner and lighter than the mini-LED models they sit alongside, and replace the notch with a Dynamic Island that hosts Live Activities, Spotlight, and Siri.

The nostalgia touches are real, too: the glowing Apple logo returns to the lid after a decade away, its brightness tied to the display. Touch costs nothing in battery life — up to 24 hours claimed — and CEO John Ternus told WIRED the Mac remains an indirect-input device first, with touch added only once it didn't make the machine heavier or thicker. Prices start at $2,899 (14-inch) and $3,399 (16-inch), with a fully maxed configuration topping $14,549. Pre-orders are open now; machines arrive November 6.

item.title: Apple's whole October lineup goes up for pre-order
item.description:
The touchscreen MacBook Pro wasn't the only thing you could buy: Apple opened pre-orders for eight new products in total. The OLED iPad mini, the M6 iMac, and the M6 MacBook Pro all arrive Friday, November 6, alongside the PROLED MacBook Pros. Still in the pipeline are the HomePod mini 2, due this Friday, October 30, and the HomeView smart home hub plus the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K, both landing November 13.

Retailers are already sweetening the deal: Best Buy is offering a $100 e-gift card with PROLED MacBook Pro pre-orders and up to $100 with the iPad mini 8 and M6 MacBook Pro, no membership required. Taken together, the week caps one of Apple's busiest Octobers ever — a new tablet display, two MacBook Pro lines, a new iMac chip, and a smart home push, all within days of each other.

item.title: Apple vs. OpenAI trade-secrets trial set for July 2027
item.description:
Judge Edward Davila has set the schedule for Apple's trade-secrets lawsuit against OpenAI, two former Apple employees, and OpenAI's io Products hardware unit, with trial slated to begin July 19, 2027. The dispute, rooted in events going back to 2019, will by then have been in litigation for about a year.

The judge also granted Apple some of the OpenAI documents it had requested, a further win in the discovery fight ahead of trial. The case is one of the highest-stakes talent-and-technology disputes in AI hardware: Apple alleges its former employees misappropriated trade secrets on their way to building OpenAI's device efforts. With the date now fixed, both sides face a long runway of depositions and document exchanges before a courtroom showdown.

item.title: South Korea fines Apple $15.5 million, orders App Store payment changes
item.description:
South Korea's media regulator fined Apple 20.8 billion won ($15.5 million) and Google 42.9 billion won ($32 million), ordering both to change app payment policies the regulator says violate a 2021 law meant to open up alternatives. Apple and Google did allow third-party payments inside apps, but charged developers a 26% commission and restricted some features — conditions regulators said pushed developers back toward the companies' own systems.

The ruling requires Apple to let developers link to external payment options from their apps. It adds South Korea to the growing list of countries chipping away at the App Store's payment model, and it lands as Apple faces similar pressure in the EU and US. Neither company has said yet whether it will appeal, but the order itself is a concrete change developers in Korea can act on now.

item.title: Russia now requires Apple to store user communications for security agencies
item.description:
Apple and Microsoft are now subject to Russian regulations requiring companies to store users' communications and hand them over to security agencies on request, according to Bloomberg. The requirement marks a significant escalation in Russia's long-running pressure on foreign tech companies to make user data available domestically.

Details of exactly what data is covered and how Apple will comply remain thin, but the stakes are obvious: a company famed for encryption and privacy marketing now faces a legal obligation in Russia that sits in direct tension with that stance. Watch for whether Apple comments publicly, and for how the rule interacts with its existing practice of storing some Russian user data locally — a compromise that has drawn criticism from privacy advocates before.

item.title: iPhone Duo tipped to take nearly 30% of the foldable market in 2027
item.description:
Apple's foldable iPhone Duo could capture nearly 30% of the global foldable smartphone market by 2027, according to a new TrendForce report, riding strong early demand for the device. That would be a remarkable debut for a company entering a category Samsung and others have spent years building — and a sign that foldables may finally be moving from niche to mainstream once Apple throws its weight behind them.

The forecast matters beyond bragging rights: a 30% share would make Apple the foldable segment's pace-setter almost immediately, pressuring rivals on price, durability, and software. It also suggests Apple's supply chain is gearing up for volume, not a cautious limited run. The usual caveat applies — analyst forecasts this far out are directional, not guarantees — but the direction of travel is clear.

item.title: Memory crunch deepens: shortages through 2030 as Mac Studio's 512GB option lands at $22,299
item.description:
Key Apple memory supplier SK Hynix warned that RAM and flash shortages are likely to last through at least 2030, keeping product prices high. Apple is reportedly one of 14 customers to have locked in priority orders, but those contracts don't shield against price increases driven by supply and demand — a warning that helps explain the creeping price hikes across Apple's lineup, including the MacBook Neo's shrinking education discount.

The same day, Apple finally opened orders for the long-promised 512GB RAM configuration of the M5 Ultra Mac Studio. The upgrade alone costs $15,500, pushing the minimum configuration to $22,299 — and to $29,799 with 16TB of storage. It's a halo machine for a tiny audience, but also a vivid price tag for the memory crunch: RAM is now the luxury option.

item.title: Apple announces the M6 iMac, its first all-in-one update in two years
item.description:
Apple's daily hardware drops continued with a refreshed 24-inch iMac, jumping straight from the M4 chip to the M6. The design, 4.5K Retina display, and seven-color lineup are unchanged, but the new machine adds Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 via Apple's N1 wireless chip, faster SSD speeds, and up to a 12-core CPU and GPU. A 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet port built into the power adapter is now available, a $30 upgrade on the base model and standard on the higher-end one.

Pricing holds steady at $1,499 for the 10-core, two-port model and $1,699 for the 12-core, four-port version — notable given recent Apple price increases elsewhere. Pre-orders open Wednesday, October 28, with availability starting Friday, November 6. For anyone still on an Intel iMac, Apple is pitching this as the moment to finally move on.

item.title: The entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro gets the M6
item.description:
Alongside the iMac, Apple refreshed the entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro with the M6 chip, keeping the same design. The M6 brings a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU (up from 10 and 10 on the M5), up to 30 percent faster graphics and 25 percent faster AI workloads, plus Wi-Fi 7, and battery life remains up to 24 hours. One quirk: the faster 170GB/s memory bandwidth only applies to the 24GB and 32GB configurations; the base 16GB model stays at 153GB/s.

Pricing is unchanged at $1,999, now with 16GB of memory and 1TB of storage standard, in Space Black and Silver. Pre-orders open October 28, with availability November 6. The higher-end M5 Pro and Max models are untouched — those await a separate, bigger redesign.

item.title: iOS 27.2 arrives, bringing Siri AI to five more languages
item.description:
After six weeks of beta testing, Apple released iOS 27.2 and its companion updates across the lineup. The headline change is Siri AI — the rebuilt, more conversational assistant — expanding to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish, with traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese promised by year's end. The EU remains excluded from Siri AI on iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch while Apple works with regulators.

The update also adds a previously delayed Messages Suggestions feature, CarPlay improvements, a new Apple Music icon, selfie-based age verification, and tvOS 27.2 features including FaceTime enhancements and shuffled screen saver categories. HomePods gain the long-awaited ability to serve as the default wireless speaker for a Mac.

item.title: Leak: touchscreen OLED MacBook Pros coming Wednesday, starting at $2,899
item.description:
This is a separate, still-unannounced product from today's M6 MacBook Pro: Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports Apple will unveil 14-inch and 16-inch touchscreen OLED MacBook Pros at its private 'Pro and Tell' event in Los Angeles on Wednesday. The new models keep the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips but add touch-enabled OLED displays with thinner bezels, a Dynamic Island replacing the notch, a new cooling system, and a lighter, slightly thinner design.

The catch is price: Apple has reportedly discussed a $2,899 starting price for the 14-inch M5 Pro model — $400 more than the current non-touch version — with the 16-inch potentially starting at $3,399 or higher. The existing non-touch models will reportedly stay on sale alongside them, positioning touch as a premium tier rather than a replacement.

item.title: ChatGPT can now read your iCloud Mail and manage your Calendar
item.description:
OpenAI added iCloud Mail and Calendar plugins to ChatGPT, bringing Apple's services to parity with Gmail and other connected accounts. With your permission, ChatGPT can search and read your iCloud Mail, manage messages and drafts, send email, look up iCloud contacts, and read, schedule, and update Calendar events that sync through iCloud.

The integration only covers Apple's own mail accounts (@icloud.com, @me.com, @mac.com) — not Gmail or Outlook accounts sitting in the iOS Mail app. It's a notable deepening of the Apple-OpenAI relationship, letting ChatGPT act on the contents of your inbox to handle scheduling, though it also hands a third-party chatbot access to some of your most personal data.

item.title: Apple Creator Studio gets its biggest update, with built-in MotionVFX and AI tools
item.description:
Apple announced a major November update to Creator Studio, its suite of pro creative apps. The biggest change: Final Cut Pro for Mac now includes MotionVFX built in, following Apple's acquisition of the plug-in maker — thousands of effects, transitions, templates, and motion graphics tools, including rotoscoping, tracking, and color grading, without a separate purchase. Final Cut Pro also gains seamless editing in Pixelmator Pro, and the curated Content Hub now includes video assets.

The update layers in AI features powered by Apple Intelligence and OpenAI models, including AI assistants and MCP support, plus a new open JSON file format for Keynote. For creators already invested in Apple's tools, it's the most substantial Creator Studio refresh since the suite launched in January.

item.title: iPhone 18 Pro sales beat last year's model globally — thanks to China
item.description:
Counterpoint Research's look at the iPhone 18 Pro's first three weeks tells a split story: global sales are up 3.1 percent over the iPhone 17 Pro, but that growth is entirely driven by China, where demand has been strong. In the US, sales are actually down 4 percent.

The regional split helps explain the conflicting narratives around the launch — analysts flagging softness while Apple still crossed a $5 trillion market valuation, with the iPhone 18 Pro apparently a key contributor. The takeaway: the Pro line's momentum is real, but it's increasingly a China story rather than a uniform global one.

item.title: Apple wins expanded evidence access in OpenAI trade secrets suit
item.description:
Apple scored another procedural win in its trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit against two former employees, OpenAI, and io Products, securing expanded access to evidence in the case. The suit centers on allegations that departing employees took confidential Apple information to their new venture.

The ruling doesn't decide the case, but broader discovery access strengthens Apple's hand as the dispute moves forward — and it lands on the same day OpenAI deepened its integration with Apple's ecosystem via the iCloud plugins, a reminder of how intertwined and adversarial the two companies' relationship has become.

item.title: Apple ships OS 27.2 across every device, with smarter Siri AI and 329 security fixes
item.description:
Apple released the first major update to its 27-generation operating systems across the entire lineup: iOS, iPadOS, macOS Golden Gate, watchOS, tvOS, HomePod software, and visionOS. The headline change is Siri AI, which can now recall past conversations and draw on more personal context like photos, calendar attendees, and voicemails, and which expands to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish, with Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese promised by year’s end. The iPhone Duo gains Apple Pencil (USB-C) support, and FaceTime Dual Capture now works in group calls.

The other reason to update promptly is security: the day’s releases patch at least 329 unique vulnerabilities in total, with more than 160 in iOS and iPadOS alone, including an Apple Intelligence flaw that could expose sensitive data. Images from Image Playground and some Apple Intelligence photo edits now also carry Google’s SynthID watermark. Older devices aren’t left out either, with iOS 26.7.2 and macOS Sequoia and Tahoe point releases landing the same day.

item.title: Apple unveils its biggest iPad mini update ever: OLED display, A20 Pro, $699
item.description:
Apple announced the eighth-generation iPad mini, calling it the biggest update the small tablet has ever received. The star is a new 8.5-inch OLED display in a thinner, lighter, slightly narrower body, powered by the A20 Pro chip, with water and dust resistance and a landscape Center Stage camera. It starts at $699 for 128GB Wi-Fi ($849 cellular), with pre-orders opening Wednesday at 10:10 a.m. Pacific.

The trade-offs: still no Face ID and no ProMotion, and the slightly changed dimensions mean some older cases may not fit. There’s also a configuration quirk worth checking before ordering — one limitation of the A20 Pro applies to all but one model. For owners of the 2024 mini, the OLED screen and chip leap are the real reasons to upgrade; everything else, from Touch ID to battery life, is largely unchanged.

item.title: The iPad mini is just day one: M6 Macs expected Tuesday, touchscreen MacBook Pro Wednesday
item.description:
Minutes after the iPad mini announcement, Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak teased an “exciting week” ahead — and the rumor mill has filled in the blanks. An M6 iMac and a 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro are expected Tuesday, with no design changes rumored for either, followed Wednesday by higher-end 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pros with touch-enabled OLED displays. Apple is holding a hands-on experience in Los Angeles on Wednesday at 10 a.m. Pacific, which explains the odd 10:10 a.m. pre-order time: a roughly ten-minute unveiling video, then orders open immediately.

If the schedule holds, this is a three-day rolling launch rather than a single event, so anyone shopping for a Mac should hold off buying until the week plays out.

item.title: Apple acknowledges iPhone Duo inner-display cracks, says only a small number affected
item.description:
After a weekend of social media reports showing cracked inner displays on the just-launched iPhone Duo, Apple issued a brief statement: the problem affects a small number of units, appears to surface relatively quickly, and anyone affected should contact AppleCare for a replacement. The company stressed that early user response to the Duo has been very positive.

The cracks share a strikingly consistent pattern, and teardown observers suspect a failing hinge element — a sheared-off part of the hinge mechanism — is behind the damage. It’s too early to tell whether this is a limited early-production defect or something broader, but the fast onset means most affected units should reveal themselves within the return window. For now, Duo owners should inspect the inner display near the hinge and keep their AppleCare options in mind.

item.title: iPhone Duo, one week in: missing eye contact, a middling repair score, and a clever Shortcuts fix
item.description:
Beyond the cracking reports, a few smaller iPhone Duo quirks surfaced this week. FaceTime’s Eye Contact setting — which subtly adjusts your gaze to look into the camera — is missing on the Duo, leaving callers looking slightly off-camera; the lack of Face ID hardware is unlikely to be the cause, since the feature doesn’t depend on it. iFixit’s teardown gave the Duo a 5/10 repairability score, the best of any foldable yet but well below the iPhone 18 Pro’s 7/10, with praise for the replaceable top screen layer offset by plenty of problem points.

On the brighter side, the Duo supports Shortcuts automations triggered by opening or closing the device, so owners annoyed that it doesn’t auto-lock when folded shut can add that behavior themselves in two steps.

item.title: The iTunes Store is making an unlikely comeback
item.description:
Seven years after Apple retired the iTunes desktop app in 2019, the iTunes Store itself is reportedly enjoying an unexpected revival. The driver is a tactic from major artists — Taylor Swift, Ariana Grande, Charli XCX, Summer Walker, and others — who are using store sales to boost chart positions and reward fans, giving the old download store a new role in an era dominated by streaming.

It’s a small story in the scheme of things, but a telling one: in a music business built on subscriptions, owning a song outright is becoming a deliberate statement again, and the store Apple supposedly left behind still has a part to play.

item.title: iPhone Duo screens are cracking along the hinge — and the hinge may be to blame
item.description:
Just days after the iPhone Duo's launch, a growing number of owners report their inner screens cracking on their own, often within hours of unboxing. The failures follow a strikingly consistent pattern: a crack down the center line of the hinge, with a horizontal block of pixels stuck glowing white afterward. Some users say they heard the hinge catch on something before the screen broke.

iFixit's teardown may have found the mechanism. The site flooded a Duo with fluorescent dust and found particles infiltrating the hinge, making it crunch — damage that could stress the display. A sheared-off piece of the hinge mechanism has also been spotted in other teardowns. Apple hasn't commented, and the failures still appear to affect a small number of units, but the consistency of the pattern has the foldable's early adopters on edge.

item.title: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook Pro arrives Wednesday with an OLED display
item.description:
Apple will unveil 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models with touch-enabled OLED displays on Wednesday, October 28, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. The announcement reverses decades of Apple refusing to put touchscreens on Macs, and attendees at Apple's "Pro and tell" experience in Los Angeles that morning will reportedly get hands-on time afterward. The laptops are said to look similar to current models but weigh less, with a Dynamic Island replacing the notch.

The hardware forces a software rethink, too: Gurman reports macOS Golden Gate will gain a dynamic, touch-friendly interface better suited to finger navigation. The touchscreen MacBook Pro is expected to carry a premium price, and it's the centerpiece of a busy week of Mac announcements.

With no design changes rumored, these look like straightforward chip-and-ship upgrades alongside the flashier touchscreen models.

Separately, the iPad mini is getting its first overhaul since 2021, with an OLED display and its first chip refresh since 2024. Between the Macs and the mini, it's shaping up to be one of Apple's busiest hardware weeks in a while — worth waiting a few days before buying any of these machines.

item.description:
Apple is testing OLED displays for future MacBook Air and iMac models, Gurman reports, but both upgrades remain some way off. The next refreshes of each machine — a new iMac expected this week and a MacBook Air refresh in early 2027 — will stick with LCD. Gurman offered no time frame for either model's OLED transition.

The picture is clear: OLED is rolling out top-down, starting with this week's MacBook Pro and the iPad mini, while the mainstream Mac lineup waits its turn. If you're shopping for an Air or iMac soon, the display technology won't be changing under you.

item.title: Apple moves to block compromised eMudhra certificates after weak keys found
item.description:
Apple is working on a macOS update with an additional fix after a security researcher discovered that private keys tied to eight intermediate certificates from Indian certificate authority eMudhra were weak. The compromised keys could have let attackers impersonate legitimate websites and put users' sensitive information at risk, though there's currently no evidence the keys were exploited.

Because eMudhra's certificates were trusted by all major browsers — Safari, Chrome, Edge, and Firefox — Apple and the other browser makers have moved to block them. It's a reminder of how much of web security rests on a handful of certificate authorities, and how quickly the whole industry has to move when one of them falters.

item.title: Apple Stores rolling out a new anti-theft check for iPhone returns
item.description:
Apple is rolling out a new anti-theft system for its retail stores, Gurman reports, aimed at a growing scam: customers buying iPhones, stripping accessories or components from the box, then returning the box hoping staff won't notice. Until now, employees were instructed to open returned boxes and verify the contents by hand.

The new system automates that box check, cutting down on wasted inventory and the awkward manual inspection. It's a small operational change, but it signals that return fraud has grown large enough for Apple to engineer its way out of it rather than just train around it.

item.title: Apple shuffles more executive roles as longtime leaders retire
item.description:
Apple is making another round of internal leadership changes as longtime executives head toward retirement, Bloomberg reports. The latest moves involve Wei Chen and John Zhong, both of whom worked on Apple's display technology — Chen took over Touch ID in 2023 when its previous head retired, and both are now reportedly stepping back from leadership.

Unlike some recent abrupt departures, this is described as a managed changeover, with Apple promoting from within to cover the roles. Still, the steady churn at the top of Apple's hardware teams is worth watching as the company heads into a major product cycle.

item.title: First iPhone Duo reviews: polished, but heavy and missing Face ID
item.description:
The first full reviews of Apple's first foldable landed on launch day, and the consensus is strikingly consistent: the Duo is beautifully polished around the edges but rough in the middle. The Wall Street Journal's Nicole Nguyen found it wider, thicker, and heavier than a Pro iPhone — heavy enough that her hand hurt after extended one-handed use — while Marques Brownlee singled out the lack of Face ID as the biggest gripe.

Third-party apps that haven't been optimized for the foldable form factor drew complaints, though one reviewer stress-tested the hinge with an industrial robot through 10,000 open-close cycles. Early adopters seem undeterred: one day-one buyer calls it a wonder to use despite its quirks and plans to daily-drive it. The verdict so far is that this is a genuinely impressive first foldable with real first-generation trade-offs.

item.title: Duo durability under scrutiny after broken screens and a failed stress test
item.description:
Launch day also brought the inevitable durability drama. A handful of early Duo units have shown up with broken inner screens, with Reddit reports pointing to a similar failure spot along the hinge and a bright line across the right side of the display. Separately, JerryRigEverything's torture test saw dust enter the hinge despite the phone's IP68 rating, overwhelming the magnets that hold it shut, before a bend test left a permanent green line and an unresponsive screen.

The important context: the problem doesn't appear widespread, and stores aren't reporting broken displays in meaningful numbers. The inner screen also only scratches at level 2 on the Mohs scale versus level 7 for the Ceramic Shield 2 outer screen — though its matte nano-texture coating makes marks appear to vanish. Worth watching, but not yet a launch crisis.

item.title: Teardowns reveal the Duo's two-battery design and 4,883 mAh total
item.description:
The first iPhone Duo teardowns are out, and they confirm the foldable splits its power across two cells: a larger 2,962 mAh battery and a smaller 1,921 mAh one, for a combined 4,883 mAh. Both cells can be removed with electrically-activated adhesive, a repairability-friendly touch.

The teardown breakdown also labels the logic board, which houses Apple's A20 Pro chip and C2 cellular modem, and shows the Touch ID sensor built into the side button — the Duo's substitute for Face ID. For a device this thin and hinge-constrained, splitting the battery across both halves is the engineering compromise that makes the whole design possible.

item.title: Three Duo tips worth knowing: Touch ID, Apple Watch unlock, and volume buttons
item.description:
No Face ID means Duo owners are rediscovering Touch ID — and the community is already optimizing it. One owner's tip, now circulating widely, is to register the lowest segment of your index finger rather than the fingertip pad, since that part rests naturally against the side button as you pick the phone up, unlocking it in one motion.

If you wear an Apple Watch (Series 9 or later, Ultra 2 or later, or SE 3), you can skip the button entirely with Unlock with Apple Watch — the closest thing to a seamless Face ID experience on the Duo. And because the foldable gets rotated constantly, a Settings option remaps the volume buttons so the top or right button is always volume up. Small fixes, but they smooth over the Duo's biggest daily friction.

item.title: Apple closes seven French stores ahead of fresh protests
item.description:
Seven Apple stores across France closed on Saturday as the country braced for another round of demonstrations, a week after looters targeted two of the company's locations. The closures include all three Paris stores — Champs-Élysées, Opéra, and Marché Saint-Germain — plus Bordeaux Sainte-Catherine, Lille, Strasbourg, and Aix-en-Provence.

The move looks precautionary: the seven locations all have entrances directly onto the street, making them harder to secure. It's a measure of how the unrest is spilling into everyday retail, with Apple choosing to protect employees and stores rather than risk a repeat of last week's looting.

item.title: Apple pushes back on DOJ bid for more evidence in antitrust case
item.description:
Apple and the U.S. Department of Justice are sparring over the scope of evidence in their antitrust case. The two sides had previously agreed to a June 20, 2025 cutoff for Apple's records, but with the evidence-gathering phase now running to late May 2027, DOJ lawyers want documents created up to 30 days before that deadline, arguing newer records could show whether the alleged anticompetitive practices are continuing.

Apple says expanding the search would delay the case by several months. The dispute is procedural, but it sets the tempo for one of the biggest antitrust fights in tech — and a longer discovery phase pushes any resolution further out.

item.title: iPhone Duo launch day brings back the lines — and the sellouts
item.description:
Apple's first foldable went on sale Friday, and launch-day lines — a ritual largely killed off by online pre-orders — returned in force. Dozens to hundreds of people queued at stores worldwide, some camping out days early, for a shot at the $1,999 device with its 5.4-inch outer display unfolding to 7.6 inches inside.

Supply is extremely tight: pre-orders slipped to January within 30 minutes of opening on October 16, and walk-in stock sold out fast. Store pickup reservations briefly resumed in Australia, China, Japan, and South Korea, but slots vanished almost immediately. In Austin, new CEO John Ternus — who took over in September — greeted the line himself, continuing the launch-day tradition in Tim Cook's absence.

item.title: First verdicts: a messy, expensive good time
item.description:
The review consensus is remarkably consistent: the Duo is genuinely fun and fresh, but compromised and buggy in first-generation ways. The Verge calls it a messy, expensive good time, noting the odd ritual of rotating the phone counterclockwise on opening so the cameras sit on top. Joanna Stern's review — which included a robot folding a unit 32,000 times in a week — lands on good, bad, and buggy, and she sorely missed Face ID.

Hands-on testers were more forgiving: AppleInsider found Apple had nearly solved its biggest form-factor concerns, and MacStories' first day, spent talking to Duo app developers in New York, felt like a slice of WWDC. The throughline is that the hardware delights while the software still catches up — a classic first-gen Apple story.

Day-one discoveries are filling in the Duo's practical picture. Only the $79 USB-C Apple Pencil works with it — Pencil 1, Pencil 2, and Pencil Pro are all incompatible. The foldable is also the first iPhone to run two apps side by side, with Split View on the inner display and the option to lock a pair so they always launch together.

Other findings: a hidden trick eases opening Control Center, developers are already shipping playful foldable apps (including a tiny retro Mac), and Apple is exploring ways to fix Safari's cramped layout on the narrow outer display. Perhaps most tellingly, the Duo ditches Face ID for a side-button Touch ID sensor, and owners can enable Rest Finger to Open to skip the swipe-up after unlocking.

item.title: Apple reclaims the world's most valuable company crown
item.description:
Wall Street liked Duo day: Apple retook the title of world's most valuable company from Nvidia on Friday, hitting new trading highs as the foldable launched. The rally capped a week of market-share gains on both sides of Apple's business.

In China, smartphone shipments fell 10% year over year in Q3 to a 14-year low, yet Apple gained ground as rising memory prices squeezed rivals. In PCs, Counterpoint estimates Mac shipments of 5.6 million units in Q3 — down 11% — but that beat a market that fell 21%, lifting Apple's share from 8.7% to 9.8%, with the MacBook Neo credited as a key contributor.
